title: Introduction to Computer System
summary: A computer is an electronic machine that takes an input, processes it and produces the desired output. Every computer is a combination of hardware and software. Hardware is the physical component that can be seen and touched (CPU, monitor, keyboard, mouse, printer). Software is a collection of programs that lets users interact with the hardware; it has a logical existence and is of two kinds: system software (operating system such as Windows 7 or Linux, antivirus) and application software (MS-Office, OpenOffice, web browsers, games). Software works as an intermediary between user and hardware.

The working of a computer has four steps: receive input (keyboard, mouse, scanner), process information (arithmetic and logical operations), store information (hard disk, CD, pen drive) and produce output (monitor, printer). Computer hardware falls into processing hardware (the CPU) and peripheral devices.
A computer has four main components: input devices, the Central Processing Unit (CPU, the 'brain' of the computer), memory and output devices.

Keyboard: like a typewriter, usually a QWERTY keyboard with 104 keys. Mouse: a pointing device that controls the cursor, with one to three buttons. Scanner: reads text or an illustration printed on paper and converts it to a form the computer can use; scanned text cannot be edited unless an Optical Character Recognition (OCR) system turns the image into ASCII characters. OCR: reads text from paper and converts it into digital form (books, magazines). MICR (Magnetic Ink Character Recognition): identifies characters printed with special magnetic ink; used in banks on cheques. OMR (Optical Mark Recognition or Mark Sense Reader): senses the presence or absence of a pencil mark; used to assess multiple-choice examinations. Bar code reader: scans the bar code of a product in supermarkets, bookshops and libraries to show its description and price. Digitizing tablet: enters drawings and sketches into a computer. Light pen: a light-sensitive detector used to select objects on the screen. Speech input devices (microphone) convert a person's speech into digital form and, with software, form voice recognition systems.

The CPU executes the instructions given to the computer; in a microcomputer it is a single chip called the microprocessor. Its parts: Control Unit (CU), which manages instructions, fetches and decodes them and directs the movement of data between memory, ALU and input/output devices; Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU), which performs arithmetic operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, shifting) and logical operations (AND, OR, NOT, comparisons); and memory registers, special high-speed storage areas that hold data and instructions temporarily during processing (often for less than a millisecond).

Monitor or Visual Display Unit (VDU) shows soft copy; it can be a CRT monitor (older, bulky, consumes more power) or a TFT-LCD/LED flat screen (light, takes less space, less electricity). Printers produce hard copy on paper: dot matrix printer (impact printer; a print head strikes an inked ribbon), ink-jet printer (non-impact; sprays ionized ink, about 300 dots per inch, line printer), laser printer (non-impact; works like a photocopier using a laser beam and toner, a page printer, 4–20 pages per minute) and thermal printer (heated pins on heat-sensitive paper, used in fax machines, low-quality print). A plotter draws charts, graphs and maps with automated pens (drum, flatbed and electrostatic plotters) and is used for CAD, CAM and CAE. Speakers give audio output through the sound card.

A bit is a 0 or 1; 8 bits make a byte. 1 KB = 1024 bytes (2^10), 1 MB = 2^20 bytes, 1 GB = 2^30 bytes and 1 TB = 2^40 bytes; 64 KB = 64 x 1024 = 32,768 bytes. Memory is primary or secondary. Primary memory (main or internal memory) is accessed directly by the CPU, is faster and more costly and loses its contents when switched off (RAM). RAM (Random Access Memory) is read/write and volatile: every location can be accessed in the same time. ROM (Read Only Memory) can only be read, is non-volatile and stores permanent programs such as the BIOS (Basic Input Output System, which starts up the computer and checks peripherals). Types of ROM: PROM (programmable once by the user), EPROM (erased with ultraviolet light and reprogrammed) and EEPROM (Electrically Erasable PROM, erased by electrical signals and partly modifiable). Cache memory is a small, very fast, expensive memory between the CPU and main memory that stores frequently used data and instructions to speed up execution.

Secondary memory (auxiliary storage) is cheaper per bit, larger and slower, and stores data permanently: magnetic tape (large volumes on mainframes, 12.5 mm to 25 mm wide and 500 to 1200 m long), magnetic disks and hard disk (stacked disks with a spindle; data recorded in concentric tracks; read/write heads on an arm), optical disks (CD-ROM, read-only, over 600 MB; CD-R, recordable once; CD-R/W, rewritable; DVD, 4.7 GB on one side, used for movies) and flash memory (non-volatile, programmed and erased in blocks, evolved from EEPROM; memory cards such as SD card, memory stick and MMC; pen drive or thumb drive connected through a USB port).
q1: Name the device which can identify characters printed with special magnetic ink and is used in banking.
MICR (Magnetic Ink Character Recognition).
April 2026
How many bytes are equal to one kilobyte?
1 kilobyte = 1024 bytes.
April 2026
Identify the scanner and the monitor from the following devices: OCR, LED, CRT, OMR.
OCR (and OMR) are scanning input devices; LED and CRT are monitors. Scanner: OCR; monitor: LED (or CRT).
April 2025
Identify hardware and software among the following: MS-Office, Mouse, Windows-7, Keyboard.
Hardware: Mouse and Keyboard. Software: MS-Office and Windows-7.
October 2025
Classify the hardware and software among the following: Monitor, Windows, MS Office, CPU.
Hardware: Monitor and CPU. Software: Windows and MS Office.
April 2024
Expand EEPROM.
Electrically Erasable Programmable Read Only Memory.
October 2025
Identify flash memories and optical disks among the following: CD-ROM, DVD, SD Card, Pendrive.
Flash memories: SD Card and Pendrive. Optical disks: CD-ROM and DVD.
October 2024
What is the 'brain of the computer'?
The Central Processing Unit (CPU), since it controls the complete working of the computer.
Name the four main components of a computer.
Input devices, Central Processing Unit, memory and output devices.
What does OMR stand for and where is it used?
Optical Mark Recognition; it assesses objective (multiple-choice) examinations by sensing pencil marks.
Which input device is used in supermarkets to read the price of a product?
A bar code reader.
Which memory is volatile: RAM or ROM?
RAM; it loses its data when power is switched off.
Name the memory that holds the BIOS.
ROM (Read Only Memory).
q2: What are the functions of the following? (i) Thermal printer (ii) Plotter

(i) Thermal printer: produces images by pushing electrically heated pins against heat-sensitive paper; used in fax machines. (ii) Plotter: draws charts, graphs, maps and engineering drawings with automated pens.
October 2025
Explain the function of the following: (i) Pendrive (ii) MICR
(i) Pendrive: a small portable flash storage device connected through a USB port to store and carry data. (ii) MICR: reads characters printed in magnetic ink, as on bank cheques.
April 2024
Define the following: (i) DVD (ii) Memory card

(i) DVD (Digital Versatile Disk): an optical disk storing up to 4.7 GB on one side, used for movies and audio-video files. (ii) Memory card: a flash memory card such as an SD card used in cameras and mobile phones.
April 2025
Explain the function of the following: (i) Barcode reader (ii) Microphone
(i) Barcode reader: scans the bar code of a product to show its description and price. (ii) Microphone: a speech input device that converts speech into digital form.
October 2024
Differentiate between hardware and software.

Hardware is the physical component (CPU, keyboard) that can be touched; software is a set of programs with logical existence (operating system, MS-Office). Both are needed; software links the user and hardware.
Differentiate between RAM and ROM.
RAM is read/write and volatile; ROM is read only and non-volatile, holding permanent programs such as the BIOS.
What is cache memory? Why is it used?
A small, very fast memory placed between CPU and main memory that stores frequently used data and instructions; it speeds up execution because the CPU is faster than main memory.
Explain the four functions of a computer.
Receive input from devices like keyboard, process information with arithmetic and logical operations, store information on devices like hard disk, and produce output through monitor or printer.
Differentiate between primary and secondary memory.
Primary memory is accessed directly by the CPU, is fast, costly and loses its data on power off; secondary memory is slower, cheaper, larger and stores data permanently (hard disk, CD, pen drive).
Differentiate between a CRT monitor and a TFT-LCD monitor.
A CRT monitor is bulky, takes more desk space and consumes more electricity; a TFT-LCD (flat screen) is light, thin and consumes much less electricity.
What is an OCR? Why is it used?
Optical Character Recognition reads text from paper and converts the image into characters the computer can edit, to digitise books, magazines and printed documents.
What is flash memory? Give two examples.
A non-volatile memory chip that retains data without power and is erased in blocks; examples are USB pen drive and SD card.
q3: Describe the various types of printers.

Dot matrix: an impact printer whose head strikes an inked ribbon to form dot characters. Ink-jet: non-impact, sprays ionized ink, about 300 dpi, better quality. Laser: non-impact page printer using a laser beam, drum and toner; 4–20 pages per minute. Thermal: heated pins on heat-sensitive paper, cheap, used in fax machines.
Explain the parts of the CPU.

The Control Unit directs and coordinates all units, fetches and decodes instructions. The Arithmetic Logic Unit does arithmetic (addition, subtraction, multiplication) and logical (AND, OR, NOT) operations. Memory registers are high-speed storage areas holding data and instructions temporarily during processing.
PROM can be programmed once by the user and never changed; EPROM can be erased with ultraviolet light and reprogrammed; EEPROM is erased with electrical signals and can be partially modified.
Describe the types of optical disks.
CD-ROM is read-only and holds over 600 MB; CD-R can be written once; CD-R/W can be written and erased repeatedly; a DVD stores about 4.7 GB per side and is used for movies.
Explain hard disk, magnetic tape and flash memory as secondary storage.

A hard disk has stacked disks with tracks and read/write heads and stores large data with quick access. Magnetic tape stores large volumes cheaply on mainframes. Flash memory is non-volatile, erased in blocks, used in pen drives and memory cards.
Describe the input devices OCR, MICR and OMR.
OCR converts printed text into digital form; MICR reads magnetic ink characters on bank cheques; OMR senses pencil marks on answer sheets of objective examinations.
Explain how memory capacity is measured. Convert 64 KB into bytes.
Memory is measured in bits, bytes (8 bits), KB (1024 bytes), MB, GB and TB. 64 KB = 64 x 1024 = 32,768 bytes.
